proposal.title: Human Rights Watch Warned Trump’s 2025 Policing Order Risked Abuse
proposal.description_short: Stop Protest Democracy Criminalization - 'Quality of Life' Weapon Against Dissent
proposal.description_medium: Human Rights Watch criticized President Donald Trump’s April 28, 2025 executive order on policing, saying it could expand mass incarceration and weaken accountability for police misconduct. The order addressed military equipment for police, prison capacity and legal protections for officers’ aggressive actions. HRW also warned about domestic use of military personnel and potential prosecution of local leaders who oppose administration policy. Its analysis does not document the protest-specific deployments, coordinated prosecutions or university funding threats alleged in the original long description.
proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump issued an executive order on policing on April 28, 2025. Human Rights Watch’s May 1 analysis said the order would increase military weaponry available to police, expand prison capacity and enhance legal protections for law-enforcement officers’ aggressive actions. HRW argued that these provisions risked expanding mass incarceration and reducing federal oversight and consequences for rights violations. The organization also raised concern about deploying military personnel in domestic law-enforcement roles and prosecuting local officials who opposed the administration’s policies. These statements are HRW’s assessment of the order and its likely consequences. They support describing an advocacy group’s warning about policing powers and accountability. The article does not document the original long description’s specific claims that officials used “quality of life” enforcement to suppress dissent, coordinated prosecutions of demonstrators, or threatened universities with funding cuts over student protests. Nor does a warning about domestic military deployment prove a protest-specific deployment. The corrected title and account therefore focus on the real order and HRW’s stated concerns, keeping the distinction between the policy provisions and the organization’s analysis of their risks.

proposal.description_long: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s office was investigating 17 cases involving federal officers during Operation Metro Surge. It documents a state-federal dispute over investigating alleged conduct during an enforcement operation. It does not connect the inquiry to a particular Trump directive or prove that a general enforcement doctrine caused it.

events.title: Gabbard Removes Two National Intelligence Council Leaders
events.description_short: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025).
events.description_medium: Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025, according to The Washington Post. The removals followed an assessment that contradicted the administration’s stated rationale for deportations; their direct role in drafting that assessment was unclear. The assessment was dated April 7 and was later partially declassified.
events.description_long: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and his deputy, Maria Langan-Riekhof, in May 2025, The Washington Post reported. Their departures came about a week after the council produced a partially declassified assessment stating that Venezuela’s government was most likely not directing the Tren de Aragua gang’s activity in the United States. That assessment undercut a rationale the Trump administration had used for invoking the Alien Enemies Act to deport alleged gang members. The Post said it was unclear whether Collins or Langan-Riekhof had a direct role in preparing the assessment, which was attributed to a National Intelligence Officer for the Western Hemisphere. The intelligence office spokesperson said Gabbard was working with Trump to end politicization of the intelligence community; lawmakers criticized the removals and warned they could chill independent analysis. The event should be stated as personnel removals following the report, while avoiding a definitive causal claim absent documentation.

events.title: CIA Fires an Unspecified Number of Probationary Recent Hires
events.description_short: Reuters reported the CIA fired more than a few probationary recent hires in early March 2025; the agency did not disclose a count.
events.description_medium: In early March 2025, the CIA fired an unspecified number of probationary recent hires, Reuters reported. The agency said it was reviewing employees in their first two years; an unnamed source said congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when dismissals began. Reuters said the dismissals began earlier that week and affected more than a few hires.
events.description_long: The CIA terminated a number of recent hires in early March 2025 as part of a review of probationary employees, Reuters reported. Three people familiar with the matter said the dismissals affected more than a few employees, but the agency did not disclose a total. A CIA spokesperson said the agency was reviewing personnel in their first two years of service and that some reviews would result in termination. The employees worked across several portfolios, and a person familiar with the matter cited performance issues as the stated basis for some terminations. Reuters also reported, based on an unnamed source, that congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when the dismissals began, despite such notification being customary. The agency’s announcement supports a discrete staffing action, but the article does not verify a specific number or that all probationary officers were fired. The held language “mass firing” overstates the public evidence; claims about required notification and national-security effects should be attributed to the cited source or experts.

events.title: Gabbard Revokes Security Clearances of 37 Officials
events.description_short: DNI Gabbard revoked clearances of 37 current and former officials; a senior CIA Russia analyst lost hers four days after the Alaska summit.
events.description_medium: On August 19, 2025, Gabbard revoked clearances for 37 officials; a senior CIA Russia analyst lost hers four days after the Alaska summit, The Washington Post reported. The memo cited alleged politicization, safeguarding failures or departures from professional standards, but did not list an individual infraction for every person named.
events.description_long: The Washington Post reported that Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard’s August 19, 2025 memorandum revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials. The memo cited alleged politicization of intelligence, failures to protect classified material or departures from professional standards, but did not identify specific infractions for every person named. Four days after the Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, a senior CIA Russia analyst was ordered to surrender her clearance, according to the Post. She had served in public intelligence work for 29 years and had an approved assignment in Europe; the clearance action ended that career. The Post reported that she had helped prepare the administration for the summit, but the reporting does not establish that the summit itself caused the revocation. The memo’s broader list and the separately reported effect on the analyst should remain attributed to the Post, and no individual misconduct should be implied absent evidence.

events.title: Trump Announces U.S. Withdrawal from Paris Climate Agreement
events.description_short: On June 1, 2017, Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Agreement; the announcement began a process rather than ending U.S. participation that day.
events.description_medium: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the 2015 Paris Agreement, saying he believed it disadvantaged U.S. workers and businesses. He said the administration would seek to negotiate a new or revised arrangement. The announcement began a withdrawal process; it did not end U.S. participation that day.
events.description_long: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the 2015 Paris Agreement, the international framework through which countries submit climate goals and report on efforts to limit warming. In his Rose Garden remarks, Trump said the deal disadvantaged U.S. workers and businesses and declared that he had been elected to represent Pittsburgh rather than Paris. He said the administration would stop implementing its emissions target and seek to negotiate a new agreement or rejoin on terms he considered fairer. The announcement began a formal withdrawal process; it did not immediately end U.S. participation in the treaty. The announcement and the treaty’s later effective withdrawal date are distinct events. The reviewed official statement supports the date, the stated economic rationale and the administration’s stated next step. It does not establish that the United States was the only country outside the pact or that the announcement was a “devastating blow” to climate diplomacy. Those unsupported or evaluative claims are omitted.

events.title: Trump Says He Directed DOJ to Terminate Remaining Biden-Appointed U.S. Attorneys
events.description_short: On February 18, 2025, Trump said he had instructed the Justice Department to terminate the remaining U.S. attorneys appointed by Joe Biden.
events.description_medium: Reuters reported that Trump announced the instruction in a Truth Social post, saying he wanted to “clean house” and restore confidence in the justice system. The Justice Department did not immediately respond. The report distinguished the February 18 instruction from termination notices sent to some prosecutors the week before and from resignations during the transition.
events.description_long: Reuters reported that Trump made the announcement in a Truth Social post, saying he wanted to “clean house” and restore confidence in the justice system. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment. The White House had sent termination notices to several Biden-appointed U.S. attorneys the week before, while others had announced resignations or left government. Reuters noted that turnover among U.S. attorneys is customary after a change in administration, though the usual practice is to request resignations rather than issue termination letters. The article separately reported that dozens of career Justice Department employees in cities including Washington and New York had been fired or quit since Trump took office; career staff are distinct from presidentially appointed U.S. attorneys. This supports a dated instruction concerning remaining Biden-appointed prosecutors, not the entry’s claim that Trump fired all U.S. attorneys and replaced them with loyalists overnight. No list of replacements is established by this source.

events.title: Trump Promotes Census Analysis Claiming Noncitizen Votes in 2020
events.description_short: Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming noncitizens voted in 2020; experts questioned its methods and said the figure could not change the result.
events.description_medium: On August 20, 2026, Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis claiming that about 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election and said it supported his claim that he won. Votebeat reported that election experts questioned the analysis because it omitted authors, detailed methods, and a margin of error. The outlet said the number, even if accurate, would not have changed the result. The Census Bureau did not respond to its request for comment.
events.description_long: On August 20, 2026, President Donald Trump promoted a Census Bureau analysis that claimed, with high confidence, that approximately 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 presidential election. He said the result supported his repeated assertion that he had won that election. Votebeat reported that experts questioned the study's reliability because it did not identify its authors, explain the data's reliability in detail, or provide a margin of error. The analysis reportedly matched voter files with federal immigration records, and the data provider said it was surprised to see its files used for this purpose. The reported 24,000 figure represented less than 0.019% of the more than 128 million voters examined. Votebeat noted that even if the number were accurate, it was too small to change the outcome; it also said the analysis could not determine whether those voters supported Trump or Joe Biden. The Census Bureau did not respond to the outlet's request for comment. These distinctions matter: the report describes a government analysis and a presidential claim, alongside expert concerns about methodology. It does not establish that noncitizen voting affected the 2020 result.

draft.description_long: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations to submit formal notice that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Agreement. It was the second time Trump had ordered a withdrawal: during his first term, the United States left the accord, and President Joe Biden later rejoined it in 2021. The 2025 order again reversed that policy and set a withdrawal process in motion; signing the order did not make the international withdrawal effective that same day. The Paris Agreement is the framework through which participating countries submit climate goals and report on efforts to limit warming. Leaving it reduces the United States’ participation in that shared process, although domestic emissions policy is also shaped by separate federal and state actions. This account focuses on the executive order and its diplomatic direction, rather than asserting unverified effects on other countries’ commitments or on U.S. emissions.

draft.title: Trump Issues Clemency Proclamation for January 6 Offenses
draft.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued a proclamation pardoning many people convicted of January 6 offenses, commuting named sentences and directing dismissal of pending indictments.
draft.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a clemency proclamation concerning offenses related to January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain defendants, commuted the sentences of named individuals, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. It was not a Justice Department motion to vacate every conviction, and pardons or commutations are legally distinct from vacating convictions.
draft.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a presidential proclamation addressing federal offenses related to events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. The proclamation granted pardons to certain people convicted of those offenses, commuted the sentences of specifically named individuals to time served, and directed the attorney general to dismiss pending indictments. These actions were executive clemency. They were not a Department of Justice motion asking a court to vacate all January 6 convictions, and the proclamation did not describe every conviction as vacated. The proclamation commuted the sentences of 14 named defendants, including Stewart Rhodes and Joseph Biggs, to time served; it pardoned all other people convicted of offenses related to January 6. It directed the Bureau of Prisons to release those held in prison immediately and ordered the attorney general to pursue dismissal with prejudice of pending indictments. proposal.description_long: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump called on the Supreme Court to limit federal judges’ authority to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration policies. Reuters reported that Trump made the appeal in a social-media post, writing “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW,” and that the Justice Department was separately asking the justices to narrow three nationwide injunctions against his birthright-citizenship order. The cases involved courts in Washington state, Massachusetts and Maryland. Trump’s statement concerned the scope of injunctions that apply beyond the parties before a court. The available reporting does not say that he declared federal judges had no authority to constrain or review the executive branch. Reuters also reported that federal courts were hearing more than 100 lawsuits against administration initiatives and that the Supreme Court’s six-member conservative majority included three Trump appointees. proposal.description_medium: On January 29, 2025, President Donald Trump directed agencies to report on existing authorities, actions and pending administrative complaints related to antisemitism at colleges and universities. proposal.description_long: The January 29, 2025 executive order directs agency heads to report within 60 days on existing authorities or actions that could be used to combat antisemitism at colleges and universities. It also asks the Attorney General to analyze pending administrative complaints involving higher-education institutions and alleged civil-rights violations connected to antisemitism, and to inventory relevant court cases and actions taken or planned. The order encourages use of existing civil-rights enforcement tools. It separately asks the State, Education and Homeland Security departments to recommend ways for universities to identify and report certain noncitizen activity relevant to grounds of inadmissibility. These are agency-review and reporting instructions. The text does not establish a new statutory definition of material support, or authorize prosecution of critics merely for criticism, donations or association. That distinction matters because the held title described a specific criminalization order that the reviewed document does not contain. The proposal retains the order’s review and reporting function while leaving possible later enforcement actions to their own evidence and dates.

proposal.description_long: On August 17, 2026, the Ninth Circuit ruled against the Trump administration’s appointment of Sigal Chattah as acting U.S. attorney in Nevada without Senate confirmation. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the court rejected an indefinite acting appointment as a way to avoid the confirmation process. The ruling left three indictments obtained while Chattah held the position intact at that stage because the appellate court could not review those prosecutions in this proceeding. Defendants remained able to raise separate challenges in later proceedings, so the decision did not dismiss or automatically invalidate the indictments. The judgment addresses Chattah’s appointment and the relief available in the appeal. It does not resolve every appointment or prosecution nationwide, and the broader claim that the court rejected all administration appointment strategy should not be inferred from this Nevada decision. For this entry, the event is the court’s ruling on the Nevada appointment; the case-specific effect on the three indictments is limited by the panel’s procedural ruling.

children.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's 2025 Continuum of Care Funding Notices
children.description_short: A federal court ruled that HUD's November and December 2025 Continuum of Care notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act and set them aside.
children.description_medium: On June 29, 2026, a federal court set aside HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices. California’s attorney general said the ruling found the notices unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act and preserved billions in homelessness funding. This decision concerned FY2025 notices; the separate August 2026 ruling addressed a later FY2026 notice.
children.description_long: A federal court ruled on June 29, 2026 that HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices could not stand. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found that HUD had made material changes to the program without following the Administrative Procedure Act. The ruling set aside the notices and preserved approximately $3.6 billion in funding for homelessness programs while litigation proceeded. The Continuum of Care program funds local and regional systems that coordinate housing and services for people experiencing homelessness. The June decision concerned the prior fiscal year’s competition and its funding notices. It should be described as a court ruling about those particular notices, rather than a blanket reversal of all HUD policy changes or a finding on every asserted consequence for people in permanent supportive housing. A later, separate August 2026 decision addressed HUD’s FY2026 notice and should retain its own date and procedural posture.

children.description_long: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked changes HUD had made to the FY2026 Continuum of Care funding competition. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found the administration’s revisions unlawful and prevented the new notice from diverting funds away from permanent supportive housing. HUD describes Continuum of Care as a competitive program that supports community systems serving people experiencing homelessness. The August ruling concerned the FY2026 notice and followed a June ruling that set aside HUD’s earlier FY2025 notices. These are separate court orders involving different annual funding competitions; they should not be collapsed into one ruling or described as three separate wins without identifying the orders. The state release characterizes the result as protecting permanent supportive housing, while the HUD competition page supplies the administrative program context. The available sources do not establish the held claim that exactly 97,000 people would be pushed onto the street.

children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to begin withdrawing from the World Health Organization. The order instructed the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to pause future transfers of U.S. government funds to WHO, recall and reassign U.S. personnel and contractors working with the organization, and suspend negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement. It also directed officials to identify alternative partners for relevant public-health activities. The order initiated a withdrawal process under the organization’s notice requirements; it did not immediately remove the United States from WHO on the day it was signed. The later decision to withdraw from UNESCO was made in a separate July 2025 announcement and under a different international organization’s procedures. The original combined title therefore conflates two actions separated by six months and involving distinct institutions.

record.title: Trump threatens to revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status
record.description_short: Trump said his administration would revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status; Harvard called the threat unlawful and unprecedented.
record.description_medium: On May 2, 2025, Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard’s tax-exempt status. Reuters described it as a renewed threat after a similar April 15 post. Harvard called revocation unlawful and unprecedented. The university was already challenging a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. record.description_long: On May 2, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard University’s tax-exempt status. Reuters reported that Trump gave no explanation in that post and described it as a renewed threat following a similar statement on April 15. Harvard responded that revocation would be unlawful and unprecedented, and said there was no legal basis to rescind its status. At the time, Harvard was already suing over a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also reported that the university had faced demands concerning governance, faculty and student viewpoints, masks, and diversity initiatives after rejecting the administration’s terms. The article distinguishes Trump’s threat from an actual IRS revocation: IRS representatives did not respond to Reuters’ questions, and the White House said any IRS action would be independent. The record should therefore describe a public threat directed at Harvard on May 2, not a completed tax-status change or a February action against multiple universities.

record.title: Trump Revokes Federal Contractor Affirmative-Action Order
record.description_short: On January 21, 2025, Trump revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed changes to federal contractor affirmative-action requirements, with a 90-day transition period.
record.description_medium: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, which revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed the Labor Department’s contractor-compliance office to cease promoting diversity and holding contractors responsible for affirmative action. The order allowed contractors to continue following the prior regulatory scheme for 90 days. It was signed January 21, not January 20.
record.description_long: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity.” The order revoked Executive Order 11246, which had governed equal employment opportunity requirements for federal contractors. It directed the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to cease promoting diversity and holding federal contractors and subcontractors responsible for affirmative action. The order also required federal contracts and grants to include terms concerning compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws and certifications about unlawful DEI programs. For 90 days, contractors could continue complying with the regulatory scheme that had been in effect on January 20. The title should therefore identify the January 21 order and its contractor provisions rather than claim that every contracting requirement ended on January 20. The White House text is primary evidence of the order’s date and terms; broader implementation effects are outside this event description.

record.description_short: Mark Danner characterizes Trump’s governing style as a “constitutional dictatorship”
record.description_medium: In his August 20, 2026 New York Review of Books essay on Regime Change, Mark Danner describes Trump’s second-term governing style as a “constitutional dictatorship.” He links the argument to expansive executive power and emergency declarations, while noting that political and practical costs sometimes prompted retreats. The phrase is his interpretation, not a court finding or formal legal status.
record.description_long: Mark Danner’s August 20, 2026 essay in the New York Review of Books reviews Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s book Regime Change and calls Trump’s second-term governing style a “constitutional dictatorship.” Danner argues that Trump expanded executive power by invoking emergencies and weakening Congress’s role, and uses the book’s reporting to discuss tariffs, immigration enforcement and other policies. He also notes occasions when Trump backed down after markets fell, courts intervened or political costs rose. The phrase is the essayist’s political characterization; it is not a court finding, legal status or description of one discrete order. The essay offers commentary on several actions and responses rather than a single event. The packet’s duplicate records carry different stored dates but cite this same NYRB essay, published on August 20. A publication-context summary should identify that essay and its argument without presenting Danner’s assessment as an established legal conclusion.

proposal.title: CREW Reports Trump Visited His Properties on 191 of 512 Days
proposal.description_short: CREW counted 191 days with Trump property visits in his first 512 days back in office, or 37%; the analysis does not substantiate the held entry’s $115 million cost total.
proposal.description_medium: A June 16, 2026 CREW analysis said Donald Trump had visited properties he owns on 191 of his first 512 days back in office, or 37%. CREW separately counted 259 individual property visits, including 148 golf-course visits, because Trump sometimes visited more than one property in a day. The article does not report the held entry’s $115 million cumulative golf-travel cost or its $300 million projection.
proposal.description_long: On June 16, 2026, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reported that Donald Trump had visited resorts and golf courses he still profits from on 191 of the first 512 days of his second term, equal to 37% of those days. CREW also counted 259 individual property visits, including 148 visits to golf courses; that number exceeds the day count because more than one property visit can occur in a single day. The article lists 102 visits to Mar-a-Lago and says Secret Service records showed nearly $100,000 spent at Trump properties in the first few months of the second term. It notes that the amount excludes costs from other agencies and discusses Air Force One operating costs by citing a Palm Beach Post analysis. The article does not establish the held entry’s $115 million cumulative travel-and-security figure or its $300 million end-of-term projection. Those totals need a separate auditable source and methodology.

proposal.title: Trump says he will always abide by courts during funding-freeze case
proposal.description_short: Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” as an appeals court rejected an emergency request in the funding-freeze dispute.
proposal.description_medium: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” while the administration challenged a lower-court order blocking a broad federal funding freeze. The First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate stay and left the district court to clarify the order’s scope. This records the February assurance; it does not support the original March claim that Trump said he could override court orders.
proposal.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.

proposal.title: DOJ Challenges Maryland Court’s Automatic Immigration Injunctions
proposal.description_short: On June 25, 2025, DOJ announced a complaint challenging a Maryland court standing order that automatically enjoined some immigration removals.
proposal.description_medium: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland over a standing order requiring automatic injunctions when detained people filed habeas petitions. proposal.description_long: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland concerning the court’s standing order on immigration habeas petitions. According to DOJ’s release, the order instructed the court clerk to automatically enter an injunction against removing or challenging the legal status of a person detained in Maryland who filed a habeas petition. The department argued that the standing order conflicted with the requirements for preliminary injunctions and with Supreme Court precedent. Attorney General Pamela Bondi said that injunctions had impeded President Trump’s agenda and described the Maryland order as judicial overreach. The public statement documents DOJ’s formal challenge to a specific court procedure and its criticism of the judiciary. DOJ described the complaint as its latest action against what it called unlawful judicial overreach. It does not establish that Bondi refused to enforce multiple injunctions, as the original entry claimed.

components.description_long: In a March 2026 analysis, the Brennan Center for Justice counted 34 emergency applications by the Trump administration to the Supreme Court during its first 14 months. The Center reported that 25 of those requests had been decided and that the administration prevailed in 80% of the decided requests. Its article compares the administration’s use of emergency applications with prior administrations, using the Center’s own case selection and classification. The figures should therefore be attributed to the Brennan Center rather than presented as an official court statistic. The analysis describes a pattern across multiple cases, not one lawsuit or a court finding that the practice was improper. It is separate from the Justice Department’s judicial-misconduct complaint concerning Chief Judge James Boasberg. That complaint was filed in July 2025 and dismissed by a judicial council in January 2026; the two events have different actors, dates, institutions and source bases.

components.description_long: The Postal Service revised its Domestic Mail Manual language on postmarks effective December 24, 2025. USPS explained that a machine-applied postmark records the date of the first automated processing operation, which may occur after the day the agency first accepted a mailpiece. The clarification described how postal possession and postmark dates can differ; USPS said it did not change longstanding postmarking practices. Customers needing a postmark on the mailing date can ask for a manual postmark at a retail counter when they tender the item, according to USPS. This is a rule clarification about mail processing and proof of mailing. It does not establish that the Postal Service changed its operations, caused late ballots, or created a nationwide ballot-delivery crisis. The broader held record also bundled postal network changes, 2026 ballot rejection reports and Executive Order 14399, which are separate events and are not substantiated by this postmark guidance. The dated clarification is therefore proposed as one component only.

components.description_long: A federal judge temporarily halted the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s planned mass layoffs in April 2025. Reuters, in a report republished by Inc., said the bureau intended to dismiss roughly 1,400 to 1,500 employees, a reduction approaching 90% of its workforce. The source therefore documents a proposed reduction and judicial intervention, not that the entire workforce was actually terminated. This April episode followed February work stoppages and preceded separate reports that some CFPB functions resumed. It should be recorded independently with the court’s temporary status made clear; the original broad claim that all enforcement matters were dropped requires a separate case-by-case review of agency and court records.

components.title: 2025 Law Narrows SNAP Eligibility for Many Lawfully Present Immigrants
components.description_short: The 2025 law restricted SNAP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants, while retaining exceptions.
components.description_medium: The 2025 reconciliation law, signed July 4, amended SNAP eligibility rules for noncitizens. NILC’s review says many previously eligible lawfully present groups—including refugees, asylees, some trafficking survivors, and certain parolees—were excluded unless they adjust to another qualifying status. Exceptions remain, and households may retain benefits for eligible members. The held title overstates the change as affecting all legal immigrants.
components.description_long: President Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, P.L. 119-21, on July 4, 2025. Section 10108 changed SNAP eligibility for noncitizens. The National Immigration Law Center’s review of the statute and USDA implementation materials says the new rule narrows eligibility for many immigrants who previously qualified, including refugees, asylees, people granted withholding of removal, some survivors of trafficking or domestic violence, certain special immigrant visa holders, parolees, and other specified groups. The law retains eligibility for lawful permanent residents, certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants, and people covered by the Compact of Free Association, with other exceptions under prior law. NILC says new applicants are subject to the restrictions immediately under USDA guidance, while households already receiving SNAP are affected at recertification; it also notes confusion in the implementation guidance. Because SNAP eligibility is household-based, eligible U.S.-citizen family members may continue receiving benefits even when another member becomes ineligible. The original wording that the law eliminated benefits for all legal immigrants is too broad.

supports: NILC’s account of narrowed eligibility, retained exceptions, new applicants/recertification timing, and household effects.

children_proposals.title: Rescissions Act cancels future Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations
children_proposals.description_short: The Rescissions Act of 2025 rescinded Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, effective upon enactment on July 24, 2025.
children_proposals.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025. children_proposals.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025, following a June 3 presidential rescission request. The enacted statute says the rescissions took effect upon enactment. Section 2(b)(20) identifies and rescinds amounts made available to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, including amounts provided through the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025. This was a statutory cancellation of specified future CPB appropriations. The law does not state that $1.1 billion was cut and does not quantify effects on individual public television or radio stations. Those amounts and downstream effects require separate appropriations records or station-level evidence. The text identifies the fiscal-year appropriations it rescinded and makes that rescission effective upon enactment; it does not itself report station receipts, local programming changes or individual broadcaster losses.

children_proposals.description_long: The White House launched a media-bias tracker webpage on November 28, 2025, according to The Washington Post. editorial_proposal.title: OCC grants World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval
editorial_proposal.description_short: OCC grants World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval
editorial_proposal.description_medium: The OCC granted World Liberty Trust Company preliminary conditional approval to pursue a national trust bank charter. The company still had to satisfy capital, governance and pre-opening requirements before it could conduct business; the letter did not authorize it to operate as a bank. Reporting raised conflict concerns but identified no finding of misconduct.
editorial_proposal.description_long: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued preliminary conditional approval for World Liberty Trust Company to pursue a national trust bank charter in August 2026. The OCC letter states that this step is not final approval and that the company may not begin banking business until it meets specified conditions and receives the agency’s final approval. Requirements include raising capital, establishing compliance and information-security policies, obtaining other regulatory approvals and requesting a pre-opening examination. If capital is not raised within 12 months or the bank does not open within 18 months, the preliminary approval expires. HuffPost reported the approval as a development involving World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company associated with the Trump family. The reports raised conflict-of-interest concerns because of that family connection, but the OCC letter does not find misconduct or say the company was already operating. The event is a conditional licensing step; whether the applicant will satisfy the requirements and receive a final charter remained unresolved.

components.title: DOJ and FBI say Epstein review found no incriminating client list
components.description_short: DOJ and FBI say Epstein review found no incriminating client list.
components.description_medium: A July 2025 DOJ/FBI memorandum said the agencies’ review found no incriminating Epstein “client list,” no credible evidence Epstein blackmailed prominent people, and no evidence to predicate investigations of uncharged third parties. The memo documents the agencies’ stated review conclusions; it does not resolve every public question about the records.
components.description_long: In a July 2025 memorandum, the Justice Department and FBI summarized their review of records related to Jeffrey Epstein. The agencies said they found no incriminating “client list,” no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence that could predicate investigations of uncharged third parties. The memorandum also reaffirmed the official determination that Epstein died by suicide in federal custody. These are the conclusions the agencies reported about the review they conducted. The document is not an independent audit of every record held by the government, does not establish that every Epstein-related record was publicly released, and is not a judicial finding about each individual associated with Epstein. The memo should therefore be described as a summary of DOJ and FBI conclusions, with the findings attributed to the agencies. Questions about records outside the review remain separate from the specific conclusions the memorandum states.

components.title: Trump asks DOJ to investigate Epstein ties of Clinton and other political targets
components.description_short: Trump said he would ask the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein's ties to Bill Clinton, JPMorgan and others.
components.description_medium: On November 14, 2025, Trump asked DOJ to investigate Epstein-related ties of Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan; DOJ said it would comply and assigned Jay Clayton. Reuters said no credible evidence linked the named individuals to Epstein’s trafficking. Reuters said the request followed House Oversight’s release of Epstein documents.
components.description_long: On November 14, 2025, President Trump publicly asked the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s connections with former President Bill Clinton, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers, investor Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan. Reuters reported that Attorney General Pam Bondi said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton would lead the investigation. The request came two days after the House Oversight Committee released a large set of Epstein-related documents and amid renewed political attention to Trump’s own past association with Epstein. Reuters reported that no credible evidence had surfaced linking Clinton, Summers or Hoffman to Epstein’s sex trafficking; the named individuals denied wrongdoing or described their contacts. This entry should report the request and DOJ’s stated response without suggesting that the investigation found crimes or that the targets had been accused of sexual offenses. It is separate from the July DOJ/FBI memorandum and the July defamation lawsuit over the birthday-note story.

components.title: Trump Declares National Emergency at the Southern Border
components.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border.
components.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Proclamation 10886, declaring a national emergency at the U.S. southern border. The proclamation directed Defense and Homeland Security officials to support border operations, including by deploying personnel and resources. It was separate from Trump’s March invocation of the Alien Enemies Act.
components.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Proclamation 10886, declaring a national emergency at the United States’ southern border. The proclamation described what it called an invasion at the border and directed the executive branch to support border enforcement using authorities and resources available under federal law. It instructed the Department of Defense to provide support for border operations and called for additional measures related to detention, removal, and physical barriers. The proclamation was a separate presidential action from Trump’s March invocation of the Alien Enemies Act. Its existence does not itself establish that every authority later used in immigration enforcement was authorized by the proclamation, nor does it describe the March deportation action. A record focused on January 20 should identify the instrument and the emergency declaration without merging it with later use of a different statute against alleged Tren de Aragua members.

components.title: Trump Invokes Alien Enemies Act Against Venezuelan Nationals
components.description_short: Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals he alleged were members of Tren de Aragua.
components.description_medium: On March 15, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals he alleged were members of Tren de Aragua. The proclamation characterized the group’s activity as an invasion or predatory incursion. It records the administration’s invocation and allegations, not independent findings about every person covered.
components.description_long: On March 15, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against Venezuelan nationals the administration alleged were members of Tren de Aragua. The proclamation described the group as engaged in an invasion or predatory incursion and stated that covered people were subject to apprehension, detention, and removal under the Act. It set out the administration’s claims about the group and its activity in the United States. Those are allegations and legal positions stated by the administration in the proclamation; they are not independent findings about every person covered or a court ruling that the Act’s statutory conditions were met. The invocation occurred almost two months after Trump’s separate January 20 proclamation declaring a national emergency at the southern border. The January proclamation invoked emergency authorities but did not itself invoke the Alien Enemies Act. These records concern two separate actions under different instruments, so descriptions and dates should not be combined into a single order.

proposal.duplicate_event_guard: Before creating either component, match existing records on date, named presidential instrument, and exact official source URL. Keep Proclamation 10886 on January 20 separate from the March 15 Alien Enemies Act proclamation; if either exact action/source is already represented, route to that record rather than create a duplicate.

components.title: Trump pardons former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean
components.description_short: On December 22, 2020, President Trump pardoned former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean, who had been convicted in connection with a 2005 shooting.
components.description_medium: The DOJ clemency record lists both agents and their convictions, including assault, firearm, and civil-rights offenses. The action occurred during Trump’s first term, not in the January 20, 2025 clemency proclamation, which concerned offenses related to the January 6 Capitol events. DOJ lists the pardon date as December 22, 2020.
components.description_long: DOJ’s official clemency records list former Border Patrol agents Jose Alonso Compean and Ignacio Ramos among President Trump’s December 22, 2020, pardons. The entries identify their convictions in the Western District of Texas and list offenses including assault with a dangerous weapon, assault causing serious bodily injury, discharge of a firearm during a crime of violence, and deprivation of rights under color of law. The page records Compean’s sentence as 144 months and Ramos’s as 132 months, with amended sentences in November 2008. Their convictions arose from a 2005 shooting incident. DOJ’s clemency page groups both pardons under the December 22 heading and lists other recipients on that date. A separate DOJ page describes the January 20, 2025 proclamation as clemency for certain offenses related to the January 6, 2021 Capitol events. The clemency action should be dated to December 22, 2020, and kept separate from the January 2025 proclamation for January 6-related offenses.
components.draft_limitation: Draft contains only facts directly supported by the cited sources.

components.title: HHS Begins Mass Layoffs Across Health Agencies
components.description_short: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs across HHS agencies, including FDA, CDC and NIH; Reuters reported plans to cut 10,000 staff.
components.description_medium: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs at several Department of Health and Human Services agencies, including the FDA, CDC and National Institutes of Health. Reuters reported that the cuts were part of a plan to reduce HHS headcount by 10,000. The reporting supports a broad health-agency reduction, not the entry’s specific claim that DOGE fired 1,500 NIH scientists in March.
components.description_long: Reuters reported that the Trump administration began mass layoffs at U.S. health agencies on April 1, 2025, after employees received dismissal notices. The cuts affected several agencies under HHS, including the FDA, CDC and National Institutes of Health, and were part of a plan reported to reduce HHS staffing by 10,000. Reuters cited multiple sources and described staff losses involving drug regulation, vaccine research, public health, and other functions. At NIH, Reuters reported that institute director Jeanne Marrazzo was fired from her post and offered another position in the Indian Health Service. The report also described staff laid off at CDC, including at least one person working on the federal measles response. It does not establish that DOGE fired approximately 1,500 NIH scientists and researchers in March or that this was one-sixth of NIH’s workforce. The substantiated event is the April 1 start of broad HHS agency layoffs.

components.title: Trump Issues Executive Order on Agency Accountability
components.description_short: On February 18, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14215, directing greater presidential supervision of executive departments and independent regulatory agencies.
components.description_medium: On February 18, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14215, “Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies.” The order addresses presidential supervision of executive departments and independent regulatory agencies and directs agency officials to consult with the attorney general on legal interpretations. Its text does not terminate an independent-counsel statute or abolish special-counsel regulations. The federal independent-counsel statute had expired in 1999.
components.description_long: On February 18, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14215, titled “Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies.” The order sets out a policy of presidential supervision over executive departments and agencies, including independent regulatory agencies, and directs agency heads to consult with the attorney general on legal interpretations. The event is an executive order about agency accountability and presidential oversight. Its text does not say that an independent-counsel statute is ended or that Department of Justice special-counsel regulations are abolished. The independent counsel provisions enacted in 1978 expired in 1999, so the claim that this 2025 order terminated that statute is also chronologically incorrect. It also required executive departments and independent agencies to submit significant proposed and final regulations to OIRA before Federal Register publication. OMB was directed to establish performance standards for independent-agency heads, while those agencies were to coordinate policy priorities with White House offices and appoint White House liaisons. The order’s text concerns executive-branch supervision and regulation review.

components.title: DHS Announces Termination of Afghanistan TPS Designation
components.description_short: DHS announced in May 2025 that Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end effective July 14, 2025; Ukraine’s TPS was extended earlier that year.
components.description_medium: A May 2025 Federal Register notice announced DHS’s termination of Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025. The notice addressed Afghanistan specifically. Separately, DHS announced in January 2025 an 18-month extension of Ukraine TPS through October 19, 2026. These were separate country-specific actions, not a March termination of TPS for millions of refugees from Afghanistan, Ukraine and other countries.
components.description_long: In a Federal Register notice published in May 2025, the Department of Homeland Security announced the termination of Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, with termination effective July 14, 2025. The notice describes Afghanistan’s earlier TPS designation and extension and explains the Secretary’s review and determination. It concerns Afghanistan and does not describe a simultaneous termination for Ukrainians, Venezuelans, Haitians, Salvadorans and other nationalities. In a separate January 2025 notice, DHS extended Ukraine’s TPS designation for 18 months, through October 19, 2026, and permitted current beneficiaries to re-register. These distinct government actions contradict the title’s combined claim that Afghanistan and Ukraine TPS were both ended as part of a March action. A corrected entry can record the later Afghanistan termination as its own discrete event, with its actual announcement and effective dates. It should not claim that all TPS protections for millions ended together.

survivor_description_proposal.description_short: Report describes DHS surveillance of Minneapolis anti-ICE protesters
survivor_description_proposal.description_medium: Court filings made public in August 2026 described Department of Homeland Security investigations of groups protesting the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. Reports said undercover agents attended meetings, entered Signal chats, recorded gatherings and obtained financial records from organizations including the Sunrise Movement and labor unions. The operation followed the January killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents. The records concern specific investigations; they do not establish that Trump personally ordered a nationwide spying program.
survivor_description_proposal.description_long: Court documents filed in August 2026 disclosed undercover Department of Homeland Security activity aimed at organizations and people protesting the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The New Republic, the Associated Press and other outlets reported that agents attended meetings, entered Signal chats, recorded some gatherings and sought financial records from groups including the Sunrise Movement, the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America. One set of documents described an undercover agent at a January 31 Sunrise Movement meeting in a public library, where participants discussed peaceful protest tactics and safety measures. The activity began after federal agents fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti during the enforcement operation, intensifying protests and scrutiny of federal policing. Prosecutors had charged a number of activists in a separate case; defense attorneys attached the investigative reports to court filings and challenged the government’s portrayal of a broader conspiracy. The records raised concerns about surveillance of protected speech and association, particularly where groups or attendees were not accused of crimes. DHS’s stated investigative rationale and the full legal basis for each subpoena remain contested. The documents demonstrate surveillance of identified groups in Minnesota, but they do not by themselves establish a single nationwide program or that President Trump personally directed the operations. The title’s original “secret police” phrase was an editorial characterization and is not used as a factual label.

The order called for review of federal actions that the administration said restricted Alaska’s resource potential and identified oil, gas, minerals, timber, and other resources. These were agency directives and review instructions, not a single immediate lease sale or completed opening of 16 million acres. The order preceded later, separately dated actions: Interior’s June 2025 NPR-A planning proposal and the October 2025 Ambler Road approval. The source documents those directives but does not substantiate the original entry’s combined acreage figure or suggest that every later project was approved on January 20.

drafts.description_long: On June 17, 2025, the Department of the Interior announced a draft management plan for the National Petroleum Reserve–Alaska. The department said its preferred alternative would make nearly 82 percent of the roughly 23-million-acre reserve available for oil and gas leasing and development, reversing protections adopted under the previous administration. The announcement was a proposed planning action: it described a draft alternative for public and agency review rather than a completed lease sale or immediate drilling authorization. The reserve was established to support petroleum development while also protecting sensitive areas and subsistence uses, so changes to its management plan affect where future leasing could occur. The original entry bundled this proposal with a January executive order and a later Ambler Road decision. Those separate actions do not share the same date or legal instrument. The draft plan supports a discrete June 2025 event; it does not establish that 16 million acres were immediately opened to drilling or that development had begun across the reserve.

drafts.description_long: In June 2025, the Federal Bureau of Prisons issued a directive addressing implementation of the First Step Act and the Second Chance Act. The bureau said the memorandum would treat First Step Act earned-time credits and Second Chance Act eligibility as cumulative and stackable for qualifying prisoners. It also said conditional placement dates should guide referrals, that stable housing and readiness for community reintegration should guide placement decisions, and that residential reentry center bed-space limits should not bar home confinement when a person is statutorily eligible. BOP described the change as intended to reduce unnecessary incarceration, ease strain on prison bedspace and staffing, and permit home confinement for qualified people with stable housing and community ties. Director William Marshall said the directive was intended to remove barriers to community placement. These are the bureau’s stated aims, not independently measured results. The announcement describes a June policy directive aimed at implementation of both statutes.

Its examples included public claims casting doubt on election integrity, appointments of election deniers to federal roles, cuts to agencies and election-security programs, demands for voter information from states, and executive orders aimed at voting procedures. The organization also warned about possible federal pressure on election certification. CAP presented these measures as a coordinated effort to consolidate power, so that interpretation should be attributed to the advocacy group rather than treated as an adjudicated finding. The fact sheet identifies concrete policy actions and proposals behind its concern, giving the record more substance than a general claim of interference. proposal.title: SSA Reports a Falling Disability Claims Backlog
proposal.description_short: SSA reported that pending initial disability claims fell 25% to 940,000 by July 23, 2025.
proposal.description_medium: On July 23, 2025, the Social Security Administration said its initial disability claims backlog had fallen to 940,000 pending cases, 25 percent below a record of more than 1.2 million the previous year. proposal.description_long: On July 23, 2025, the Social Security Administration reported that its initial disability claims backlog had fallen to 940,000 pending cases. SSA said this was a 25 percent reduction from a record of more than 1.2 million cases the previous year. The agency attributed service changes to new telephone technology, process engineering and resource alignment. It also reported faster customer service: its National 800 Number handled nearly 1.3 million calls the prior week, 70 percent more than in the comparable week a year earlier, while the average wait to speak with an agent was six minutes. SSA said field office wait times averaged 23 minutes so far that year, compared with 30 minutes in the prior year. The release further reported that the number of pending disability hearings remained at historic lows and average hearing waits had fallen by 60 days since June 2024. These are agency-reported service figures and do not establish the separate claim that millions newly faced crippling delays after July DOGE cuts. The narrow event supported here is SSA’s July 23 public report on service performance and backlog reduction.

proposal.title: BLS Reports August 2025 CPI Rose 2.9% Over the Year
proposal.description_short: BLS reported August 2025 CPI rose 0.4% monthly and 2.9% over 12 months.
proposal.description_medium: On September 11, 2025, BLS reported that the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers rose 0.4 percent in August and 2.9 percent over the 12 months ending that month. Shelter was the largest contributor to the monthly increase; food rose 0.5 percent and energy 0.7 percent. The release does not support the original 6 percent figure or establish that tariffs caused the change.
proposal.description_long: On September 11, 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Consumer Price Index for August. The CPI for All Urban Consumers increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis during the month, following a 0.2 percent increase in July. Over the 12 months ending in August, the all-items index rose 2.9 percent before seasonal adjustment. The shelter index rose 0.4 percent and was the largest factor in the monthly increase; food rose 0.5 percent and energy rose 0.7 percent. The index for all items less food and energy increased 0.3 percent in August and 3.1 percent over 12 months. BLS also reported gasoline prices rose 1.9 percent in the month. The official release therefore contradicts the entry’s claim that consumer prices surged 6 percent in August. The event can be retained as a dated statistical release, while any claim about tariff effects requires separate evidence and should not be conflated with the aggregate CPI result.

proposal.title: Trump Issues Covington Memorandum on Clearances and Contracts
proposal.description_short: A February 25, 2025 presidential memorandum directed reviews of specified Covington clearances and federal contracts.
proposal.description_medium: On February 25, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a memorandum directing agencies to suspend specified security clearances held by Covington personnel who assisted former special counsel Jack Smith, end firm engagements where lawful, and have OMB review government contracts with the firm. The memorandum states directives; it does not show that each was carried out.
proposal.description_long: On February 25, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a presidential memorandum addressed to the Secretaries of State, Defense and Energy, the attorney general, and the directors of several intelligence, personnel and budget agencies. The memorandum directed agencies to suspend, pending review, active security clearances held by Peter Koski and Covington & Burling members, partners or employees who had assisted former special counsel Jack Smith. It also instructed agencies to end the firm’s government engagements to the maximum extent permitted by law, asked OPM to circulate the memorandum to other clearance-granting agencies, and directed OMB to issue guidance for reviewing federal contracts with Covington. Each directive was qualified by applicable law. The White House text establishes what the memorandum ordered; it does not establish that every clearance was suspended, every contract was terminated, or that a review found misconduct. The document was a presidential memorandum, not the March 14 executive order described in the original entry. The proposed record reports the issuance and terms of the memorandum, not its later implementation.

proposal.title: Deutsche Bank Group Finances Chicago Trump Tower in 2005
proposal.description_short: In 2005, a lender group including Deutsche Bank made a $640 million construction loan for Trump International Hotel and Tower in Chicago, The Washington Post reported.
proposal.description_medium: The Washington Post reported that a Deutsche Bank-led group made a $640 million commercial construction loan for Trump International Hotel and Tower in Chicago in 2005. It was one project loan, distinct from later private-wealth loans for Doral and the Washington hotel. A 2008 payment dispute led to litigation; the parties settled in 2009. The report does not establish that the loan was an aggregate across Trump properties or involved foreign-intelligence leverage.
proposal.description_long: In 2005, Deutsche Bank and other lenders provided a $640 million construction loan for Trump International Hotel and Tower in Chicago. The Washington Post reported that this was one commercial real-estate loan and that the bank later syndicated much of it, reducing its own exposure. In 2008, Trump did not pay $334 million due on the loan and sued Deutsche Bank, arguing that the financial crisis was unforeseeable and seeking $3 billion in damages. The parties settled out of court in 2009, and the bank’s commercial mortgage unit did not do business with Trump again. The Post described the earlier relationship as including a separate $125 million 1998 loan for 40 Wall Street and another loan for Trump World Tower. Later loans for Doral and the Washington hotel came from Deutsche Bank’s private-banking division. The Chicago loan date is reported only by year. The proposed entry keeps that single commercial loan distinct from other properties and financing arrangements; it does not imply an aggregate $640 million loan package, foreign-intelligence leverage, or concealed subpoena information.

proposal.title: Iran Fires Missiles at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar
proposal.description_short: Iran fired missiles at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar on June 23, 2025; U.S. and Qatari defenses intercepted the attack.
proposal.description_medium: On June 23, 2025, Iran fired missiles toward Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar after U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites. ABC News reported that U.S. and Qatari defenses intercepted the attack, no Americans were harmed, and Trump said 13 of 14 missiles were knocked down. The reviewed reporting supports one target, not attacks on several bases.
proposal.description_long: On June 23, 2025, Iran fired missiles toward Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest U.S. military base in the region, after U.S. strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities. ABC News reported that a U.S. official said American forces intercepted the missiles with Qatari assistance. President Donald Trump said 13 of 14 missiles were knocked down and that one was allowed to continue because it was traveling in a nonthreatening direction. Trump reported no American casualties and little damage. ABC also reported that Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, wrote after the attack that Iran would not surrender. The account establishes a single attack targeting Al Udeid. It does not substantiate the original record’s claims of simultaneous strikes on bases in Iraq, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates or three U.S. personnel killed. The attack followed U.S. strikes on June 21 and 22, rather than taking place on June 14 as the held entry states. The revised record should attribute the interception and casualty statements to the reporting or named speaker.

proposal.title: HHS Removes 17 Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Committee
proposal.description_short: HHS said it removed all 17 sitting ACIP members on June 9, 2025 and would replace them with members then under consideration.
proposal.description_medium: On June 9, 2025, HHS announced that it had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and would replace them with members then under consideration. ACIP advises CDC on vaccine safety, efficacy and clinical need. The announcement supports a dated membership action, not the held entry’s February 10 date.
proposal.description_long: On June 9, 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services announced that Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the panel that advises the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on vaccine safety, efficacy and clinical need. HHS said it would replace the members with people then under consideration and described the action as a total reconstitution of the committee. The department also said ACIP was scheduled to meet June 25–27 at CDC headquarters in Atlanta. This proposal records HHS’s dated membership announcement and attributes the department’s description to HHS. It does not establish that the committee had been dissolved, that the action occurred on February 10, or that the change eliminated independent scientific oversight or endangered the public. Those broader statements in the held synopsis are not substantiated by the cited source. The corrected date is June 9, 2025, and the source supports the membership change, not the effects of future committee advice.

proposal.title: New York Appeals Court Modifies Trump Civil-Fraud Judgment
proposal.description_short: A divided New York appeals court vacated disgorgement awards in the Trump civil-fraud case but otherwise affirmed parts of the judgment.
proposal.description_medium: The New York Appellate Division’s August 21, 2025 opinion describes trial findings that Trump and Trump Organization entities submitted deceptive financial statements to lenders and others for business benefits, including favorable loan terms. The divided appellate court vacated disgorgement awards and otherwise affirmed portions of the judgment. This was not a loan made by the organization to Trump personally.
proposal.description_long: On August 21, 2025, New York’s Appellate Division, First Department, issued a divided decision in People v. Trump, the state civil-fraud case involving statements of financial condition prepared by Donald Trump and Trump Organization executives. The opinion describes the trial court’s finding that defendants repeatedly submitted deceptive business records to lenders, insurers and other counterparties to obtain financial benefits. The appellate court modified the judgment to vacate disgorgement awards and otherwise affirmed parts of it; separate opinions disagreed about aspects of the analysis and remedy. The case involved financial statements and business loans connected to Trump Organization entities, including transactions supported by personal guarantees. It was not an event in which the organization lent money to Trump personally at favorable rates, and the opinion should not be described as an unqualified final decision on every claim in the original record. The revised entry is limited to the dated appellate disposition and the scope of the court’s ruling. It preserves the divided procedural result rather than flattening it into a single finding.

proposal.title: Trump Calls MS-13 Members “Animals” at California Roundtable
proposal.description_short: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable, Trump said “These are animals” during a discussion of MS-13 gang members.
proposal.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable about California sanctuary policies, President Donald Trump discussed MS-13 gang members and said, “These are animals.” The archived transcript places the phrase directly after his reference to MS-13. This supports a contextualized account of the remark, not the claim that he described immigrants generally as animals.
proposal.description_long: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable on California sanctuary policies, President Donald Trump discussed immigration enforcement and members of the MS-13 gang. The archived transcript places his phrase, “These are animals,” immediately after remarks about MS-13. The exchange followed Sheriff Margaret Mims’s account of a possible gang member whom local authorities could not report to ICE under a sanctuary-policy threshold. Trump then broadened his remarks about people entering the country before repeating, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” The transcript establishes the setting, wording and immediate context, but it does not support a title saying he called immigrants collectively “animals.” It also does not place the remark at a 2019 rally. This proposal ties the claim to the cited passage and avoids inferring a broader referent than the transcript demonstrates. The archived record is primary evidence of what was said at the roundtable; it does not resolve how every listener interpreted the wording.

draft.title: Knowles Fire burnover kills three federal firefighters
draft.description_short: Knowles Fire burnover kills three federal firefighters.
draft.description_medium: On June 27, 2026, five federal wildland firefighters were caught in a burnover during initial attack at Colorado’s Knowles Fire. The Department of the Interior reported that three died at the scene and two were injured. Its account documents the incident and casualties but makes no finding that staffing cuts, prescribed-fire reductions or suppression policy caused the burnover.
draft.description_long: On June 27, 2026, five federal wildland firefighters were caught in a burnover while working on initial attack at the Knowles Fire in western Colorado. The Department of the Interior reported that three firefighters died at the scene and two others were injured. Its account identifies the incident as the Knowles Fire and documents the immediate casualties; it does not establish that Forest Service staffing reductions, prescribed-burn acreage or a 2026 suppression directive caused the burnover. Those broader policy claims in the original entry go beyond the official facts cited for this incident. The department later reported that one of the injured firefighters died on July 24, raising the incident’s fatality count to four. That later death is a separately dated development connected to the same burnover, not a second fire or a separate initial-attack event. This proposal corrects the “Snyder Fire” identification, separates the June 27 incident from the later fatality update and leaves causation open pending an investigation finding. No accident-investigation conclusion is included in the cited source.

draft.title: Fourth Knowles Fire firefighter dies from burnover injuries
draft.description_short: Fourth Knowles Fire firefighter dies from burnover injuries.
draft.description_medium: On July 24, 2026, Nathan Matthews died from injuries sustained in the June 27 Knowles Fire burnover, the Department of the Interior reported. His death raised the incident’s fatality total to four. The department said its accident investigation remained underway; the release did not assign a cause to the burnover.
draft.description_long: On July 24, 2026, Nathan Matthews died from injuries sustained in the June 27, 2026, burnover at Colorado’s Knowles Fire, according to the Department of the Interior. His death brought the number of firefighters killed in that incident to four. The department had previously reported that five federal wildland firefighters were caught in the burnover while working on initial attack; three died at the scene and two were injured. The later release said an accident investigation remained underway. It supports the identity, date and outcome of Matthews’s death, but it does not provide a finding that attributes the burnover to federal staffing levels, prescribed-fire acreage, drought or suppression policy. The original entry combined this later death with a disputed fire name and broad policy claims. This proposal treats July 24 as the date of the fatality update, preserves its link to the June 27 incident and leaves the incident’s cause unresolved until the investigation produces a supported finding.

draft.title: Trump dismisses NSA and Cyber Command chief Timothy Haugh
draft.description_short: Trump dismissed NSA and Cyber Command chief Timothy Haugh amid a White House loyalty-purge episode.
draft.description_medium: Reuters reported that President Donald Trump dismissed Timothy Haugh, who led the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command, on April 4, 2025.
