draft.description_long: On April 4, 2025, President Donald Trump dismissed Gen. Timothy Haugh, the director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command, Reuters reported. The article described the decision in the context of a White House loyalty-purge episode and said activist Laura Loomer had advocated removing officials she considered disloyal. This supports the timing, Haugh’s roles and the reported political context; it does not show that Loomer made the decision, that she ordered Haugh’s firing, or that the removal caused later cyber incidents. The original record combines Haugh’s dismissal with an August action by Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to revoke clearances held by 37 intelligence professionals. That later action is separate by date and actor. The cited Reuters article for April does not substantiate the August details or the asserted link between the events. The proposal therefore splits the April dismissal into a narrowly framed report and leaves the August claim on hold pending a directly read Reuters article or official document plus complete descriptions.

draft.title: Trump calls for terminating constitutional rules after 2020 election
draft.description_short: Trump called for terminating constitutional provisions to overturn the 2020 election and return him to power.
draft.description_medium: In a December 3, 2022, Truth Social post, Donald Trump called for ending rules, regulations and constitutional provisions to overturn the 2020 election and restore him to power. CNN quoted the post and reported that it followed the release of internal Twitter emails about the platform’s handling of a New York Post story concerning material from Hunter Biden’s laptop.
draft.description_long: On December 3, 2022, Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that a “Massive Fraud” in the 2020 election allowed for the termination of all rules and regulations and even articles in the Constitution. He asked whether the 2020 results should be discarded and a new election held, or whether a “rightful winner” should be declared, and said this would return him to power. CNN quoted the post and reported it followed the release of internal Twitter emails about the platform’s handling of a New York Post story about material from Hunter Biden’s laptop. The article recorded responses from White House spokesman Andrew Bates and Rep. Liz Cheney, who condemned the statement. Those responses are attributed reactions. The post was a political statement; it did not itself change constitutional law, reverse the 2020 election or reinstate Trump. This proposal removes claims about its lasting centrality or later impact that require separate evidence. Entry 5385 describes the same December 3 post, so use it as the sole event record and consolidate this duplicate into that survivor.

draft.title: Trump announces U.S. withdrawal from Paris Climate Accord
draft.description_short: Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord and seek a new deal.
draft.description_medium: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord and said he would seek a new agreement on terms he considered fair. The archived White House transcript records his stated rationale; it does not establish the diplomatic effects or environmental consequences of the announced policy.
draft.description_long: On June 1, 2017, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord. In the archived White House transcript, he said the country would stop implementing the agreement and that his administration would begin negotiations to reenter the accord or pursue a new arrangement on terms he viewed as fair. Trump argued that the agreement disadvantaged U.S. workers and businesses; those claims are his stated rationale, not independently verified effects. The transcript establishes what the president announced and the case he made in the speech. It does not substantiate claims that the announcement isolated the United States diplomatically, caused particular international reactions, or reflected hostility to environmental science. This proposal narrows the entry to the dated withdrawal announcement and attributed rationale, excluding those broader interpretations. A second held record, entry 5632, covers the same June 1 announcement and should remain the single event record after consolidation. No separate diplomatic outcome is inferred from the statement alone.

draft.title: Education Department Starts RIF Affecting About 1,300 Positions
draft.description_short: Education announced a March 11 RIF affecting nearly half its workforce; OIG later counted 1,227 RIF and 352 voluntary departures by March 31.
draft.description_medium: The Education Department announced a reduction in force on March 11, 2025, affecting about 1,300 positions and placing impacted staff on administrative leave. The department’s own release said its workforce would shift from 4,133 to roughly 2,183, a projection that also reflected voluntary departures. Education OIG later reported 1,227 RIF separations and at least 352 voluntary separations through March 31, 2025. The held entry’s count should not be presented as 1,300 completed firings.
draft.description_long: On March 11, 2025, the U.S. Department of Education announced that it had initiated a reduction in force affecting nearly half of its workforce and that impacted employees would be placed on administrative leave. The department’s release described its workforce as 4,133 at the start of the administration and projected roughly 2,183 after the actions. That projection included employees who had already accepted voluntary separation programs as well as the new RIF. The Department of Education Office of Inspector General later reported staffing changes in 16 of 17 offices and an overall reduction of at least 1,579 of 3,902 employees by March 31, 2025: 1,227 employees separated through RIF actions and at least 352 through voluntary options. GAO separately documented that about half of the Office for Civil Rights staff were placed on paid administrative leave and that later court orders affected the RIF. The original statement that DOGE fired 1,300 employees should be replaced with an accurately attributed announcement and counts distinguishing positions affected, completed RIF separations, and voluntary departures.

draft.title: Trump Media plans a paid early-access feed for Truth Social posts
draft.description_short: Trump Media plans a paid early-access feed for Truth Social posts
draft.description_medium: Trump Media & Technology Group planned a paid Truth API feed offering early access to Trump’s Truth Social posts for up to $100,000 per month. Opinion writers argued that the service could privatize public presidential records and weaken public access; those are legal and ethical arguments, not an official finding that the feed is unlawful.
draft.description_long: Trump Media & Technology Group announced a paid, licensed Truth API feed intended to give banks and trading firms faster access to posts from the ten most influential Truth Social accounts. Reuters reported that, before the launch, the company had discussed charging up to $100,000 per month, or $60,000 monthly for a three-year commitment. Reuters also reported that the company said customers had signed up ahead of launch, but did not identify them; the reported offer prices came from unnamed sources. The product raises questions about whether financial firms can receive Trump’s posts before ordinary users and news outlets, particularly when posts announce tariffs or other government actions. A press-freedom group and a media outlet later sued, arguing that the feed sold government information; Trump Media responded that the posts were widely available. The sources establish a commercial data product and reported pricing, but they do not provide an official determination that each post is a presidential record or establish that the service violated records law. The legal status of the posts and the boundaries between the company’s feed and government records remain unresolved.

draft.title: The Independent analyzes Trump administration election actions and court setbacks
draft.description_short: The Independent analyzes Trump administration election actions and court setbacks
draft.description_medium: An August 2026 Independent analysis reported that Trump’s efforts to expand federal control over elections had faced court defeats, congressional resistance, and state-level opposition ahead of the midterms. draft.description_long: The Independent’s August 17, 2026 analysis described several routes the Trump administration had pursued to gain influence over federal elections and the legal and political obstacles they encountered before the midterms. It reported that the Justice Department had lost more than 20 cases seeking state voter data, that federal courts had blocked executive orders concerning mail ballots and a national voter-identification policy, and that Congress had not advanced the SAVE America Act. The article also discussed the administration’s possible next moves, including Trump’s suggestion of a national emergency focused on election security and efforts to seek Supreme Court intervention. Its account places those actions against the constitutional division of election responsibilities between states and Congress and notes concerns from election officials about late changes to voting rules. The article is political analysis; its descriptions of the administration’s objectives and the likely consequences are attributed interpretations, not court findings that a plan to seize control succeeded.

draft.title: Trump Sells Early Access to Truth Social Posts
draft.description_short: Trump Sells Early Access to Truth Social Posts
draft.description_medium: Donald Trump is selling early access to his Truth Social posts, a move that is being criticized as a clear example of grift and financial exploitation. The move is seen as a way for Trump to make money, but critics argue that it is unfair and potentially corrupt.
draft.description_long: The Philadelphia Inquirer editorial board reported on August 18, 2026, that Trump Media was selling investors advance access to Trump’s Truth Social posts for as much as $100,000 per month. The editorial argued that previews of posts capable of moving markets could give subscribers an informational advantage and raise insider-trading concerns. It also criticized the absence of a visible federal investigation. Those are the editorial’s concerns, not findings that an investor traded on a preview, that a law was violated, or that regulators reached a conclusion. Early access to a president’s public communications may raise serious questions, but the report names no subscribers and gives no comparison of subscriber access times with public posts. The offering tied a commercial service to Trump’s social-media activity. Its practical effect and legal significance depend on how the previews worked and whether anyone used them to trade.

draft.title: Trump Administration Interfering in 2026 Midterm Elections
draft.description_short: Trump Administration Interfering in 2026 Midterm Elections
draft.description_medium: The Center for American Progress argued that the Trump administration was using several methods to influence the 2026 midterms. Its fact sheet lists efforts involving election-denier appointments, federal voter data, agency cuts and executive orders affecting voting access. These are CAP’s claims and framing, not court findings.
draft.description_long: The Center for American Progress published a fact sheet on August 19, 2026, arguing that the Trump administration was using a multipronged strategy to shape the 2026 midterm elections. Its examples included public claims casting doubt on election integrity, appointments of election deniers to federal roles, cuts to agencies and election-security programs, demands for voter information from states, and executive orders aimed at voting procedures. The organization also warned about possible federal pressure on election certification. CAP presented these measures as a coordinated effort to consolidate power, so that interpretation should be attributed to the advocacy group rather than treated as an adjudicated finding. The fact sheet identifies concrete policy actions and proposals behind its concern, giving the record more substance than a general claim of interference. It does not establish that every measure would alter election results, that all described actions were implemented, or that a court had found the administration violated election law. The sourced account is therefore a report of CAP’s allegations and examples, with the legal and electoral effects left open.

proposal.proposed_title: The Atlantic Selected 50 Norm-Bending Moments From Trump’s First Two Years
proposal.proposed_description_short: The Atlantic’s 2019 project selected 50 incidents from Trump’s first two years and described them as improbable, norm-bending and destructive.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: The Atlantic’s January 2019 “Unthinkable” project selected 50 moments from Donald Trump’s first two years in office. The editors described the choices as improbable, norm-bending and destructive and said the ranking was subjective. An interview with editor Adrienne LaFrance explains the project’s editorial lens. These sources document the magazine’s framing, not an independent adjudication of every incident.
proposal.proposed_description_long: In January 2019, The Atlantic published “Unthinkable,” an editorial project surveying Donald Trump’s first two years in office through a ranked list of 50 incidents. The page says editors began with hundreds of moments and selected incidents they considered improbable, norm-bending and destructive; it also describes the ranking as subjective and based on both outlandishness and importance. The entries include examples concerning Trump’s public remarks and treatment of institutions. In a contemporaneous WBUR interview, Atlantic editor Adrienne LaFrance discussed the project and explained its editorial lens. Together, these sources support a description of what The Atlantic chose to catalog and how it framed its selections. They do not independently adjudicate every event on the list or substantiate a separate claim that the administration made structural reforms, or that a defined institutional pattern was officially recognized. Keep the article’s evaluative terms attributed to the magazine and avoid presenting its editorial ranking as an objective measurement. The corrected title identifies the project and its selection of 50 moments without turning the magazine’s framing into a broader factual conclusion.

proposed_fields.description_long: On February 3, 2025, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan of the District of Columbia issued a temporary restraining order in litigation over the Office of Management and Budget’s federal-assistance freeze. The court order says it granted the plaintiffs’ motion for a TRO and denied the administration’s motion to dismiss. NPR reports that the injunction blocked the administration from implementing, giving effect to, or reinstating the original OMB directives under another name, and said previously frozen open awards had to be released. The order arose after OMB’s January 27 memorandum directed agencies to review federal financial-assistance programs and temporarily pause covered activity. The court action was a temporary restraint during litigation; the cited sources do not describe a government shutdown or an injunction against firing federal employees. The original title and short description refer to shutdown-related firings, while the linked reporting and court order concern the separate funding-freeze dispute. This revised account identifies the court, date, instrument, and scope, and avoids describing the TRO as a final merits judgment.

preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump systematically eliminated disability rights protections by gutting Americans with Disabilities Act enforcement, ending Medicaid funding that enabled community living, and removing 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that had addressed systemic ableism while forcing disabled Americans back into institutional settings through funding cuts and accommodation elimination. The comprehensive disability rights destruction represented Trump's implementation of Project 2025's plan to eliminate federal regulations and programs that supported independent living, with $880 billion in Medicaid cuts that would 'strip coverage from 17 million people' including disabled Americans who relied on federal healthcare for wheelchairs, ventilators, personal care attendants, and community-based services. The ADA rollback included eliminating 'disparate impact' discrimination protections that addressed unintentional but systematic bias against disabled people, while removing federal requirements for businesses, educational institutions, and government agencies to provide reasonable accommodations that ensured equal access and participation. Trump's disability targeting violated constitutional equal protection principles by removing legal tools that disabled Americans used to 'highlight ableism within institutions' and seek redress for discrimination, while Medicaid cuts forced disabled people 'out of their homes and into hospitals and nursing homes' against their will and constitutional rights. The disability rights elimination created what advocates called return to 'earlier, shameful era of isolation, exclusion, and institutionalization' by removing Olmstead protections that affirmed disabled people's right to live in community settings with appropriate supports rather than segregated institutional facilities. The systematic accommodation destruction represented Project 2025's vision of society that abandoned federal responsibility for disability inclusion, transforming disabled Americans from equal citizens with supported rights into vulnerable populations subject to institutional control and social exclusion through elimination of legal protections and community-based services.

staged_description_snapshot.description_long: On November 4, 2024, Axios reported that Donald Trump’s campaign had prepared staff for either result in the upcoming presidential election. The report described an internal “Donald J. Trump Administrative Update” from co-campaign manager Susie Wiles. It said November 30 would be the staff’s last day on payroll regardless of the outcome and that, if Trump and JD Vance won, some employees would move to the official transition or Presidential Inaugural Committee. Axios also reported that Trump told ABC News correspondent Jonathan Karl he expected to win, while acknowledging that he could lose. Trump spokesperson Karoline Leavitt separately characterized the work as preparation for a successful transition following victory. These facts support a specific account of campaign wind-down and transition planning before Election Day. They do not substantiate the earlier TrumpFile assertion that Trump never planned to win. The Axios article was published after that August post and concerns a distinct late-campaign event; its contingency plans cannot establish Trump’s earlier private intentions. The original allegation should remain unverified and should not be presented as fact.

staged_description_snapshot.title: Trump's 'Covfefe' Tweet Stayed Online for Nearly Six Hours
staged_description_snapshot.description_short: Trump posted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” just after midnight on May 31, 2017; he deleted it about 5:50 a.m. after it became an online joke.
staged_description_snapshot.description_medium: At 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017, Donald Trump tweeted, “Despite the constant negative press covfefe,” an unfinished sentence that drew widespread attention. The Washington Post reported that he deleted it at 5:48 a.m.; Trump later asked followers to guess its meaning. The episode supports a description of the post and reaction, not broader claims about policy or presidential competence.
staged_description_snapshot.description_long: Donald Trump posted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” at 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017. The Washington Post reported that the fragment drew rapid attention and became an internet joke; it was retweeted more than 127,000 times and liked more than 162,000 times within six hours, according to the newspaper’s contemporaneous account. The tweet was deleted at 5:48 a.m. Eastern. Trump then posted, “Who can figure out the true meaning of ‘covfefe’???” USA Today’s one-year retrospective likewise says the original post was an unexplained partial sentence, remained online for nearly six hours and was followed by Trump leaning into the joke rather than explaining the original wording. The records support the timing, exact text and public reaction. They do not establish what Trump intended to write or that the post caused a policy or institutional consequence. This revised description replaces “incomprehensible” with observable facts and keeps the entry to the social-media episode documented by the cited reports.

staged_description_snapshot.description_medium: A Senate Judiciary Committee release says Sen. staged_description_snapshot.description_long: In a Senate Judiciary Committee press release, Sen. Dick Durbin, the committee’s ranking member, said he had received whistleblower information about FBI Director Kash Patel’s use and management of bureau aircraft. Durbin characterized the disclosures as alleging that aircraft decisions affected or delayed high-profile investigations, including the Charlie Kirk killing. As an example, he said the FBI shooting-reconstruction team was asked to fly to Utah to assist with the investigation and process the scene. The release does not provide flight logs, a detailed response timeline, or an independent inspector general finding establishing that Patel’s personal travel delayed that team. It does make a separately worded allegation about the FBI’s response to the Brown University shooting, which should not be conflated with the Kirk investigation. The supportable entry is that a senator publicly disclosed whistleblower allegations and described a requested deployment after Kirk’s killing. It should not state as proven fact that personal aircraft use hampered the Kirk response or multiple emergencies. The FBI’s contemporaneous account says agents arrived at the scene within 16 minutes, a distinct fact that further cautions against overstating the alleged delay.

account1_source_proposal.proposed_title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria visit to Puerto Rico included paper-towel distribution
account1_source_proposal.proposed_description_short: Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria included a paper-towel distribution at a relief center.
account1_source_proposal.proposed_description_medium: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017. Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to people at a relief center. GAO later found that staffing, logistics and infrastructure problems complicated FEMA’s response. A George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths through August 2018; this is an excess-mortality estimate, not a count of deaths individually attributed to the storm. The evidence does not connect the paper-towel scene to response delays.
account1_source_proposal.proposed_description_long: Hurricane Maria made landfall in Puerto Rico in September 2017 and caused widespread damage to infrastructure, housing and communications. President Donald Trump visited the island on October 3. During a stop at a relief center, he tossed rolls of paper towels to people gathered there, an action that attracted criticism and became a prominent image of the visit. The federal response faced documented operational problems. The Government Accountability Office later reported that sequential disasters created staffing shortages, logistical challenges impeded the rapid deployment of personnel and supplies, and damage to local systems required FEMA to assume functions normally handled by territorial authorities. Separately, a George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths associated with Hurricane Maria through August 2018; GAO described that figure as Puerto Rico’s then-current official count. “Excess deaths” compares observed deaths with an expected baseline and should not be conflated with a count of deaths individually certified as directly caused by the storm. These sources support the visit, the distribution scene, response challenges and the later mortality estimate. They do not establish that the paper-towel event caused FEMA delays, nor do they provide support for every claim about the Jones Act or funding transfers in the original description. The title is narrowed to the documented visit; the response and mortality context is stated with attribution.

proposed_fields.description_long: On January 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14187, titled “Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation.” The order defines a child as a person under 19 and describes puberty blockers, certain hormones and some surgical procedures as the care it seeks to restrict. It directs federal agencies to take steps involving grants and federal health programs, including TRICARE, and instructs the attorney general to prioritize enforcement of laws the order says prohibit or limit the procedures. Human Rights Watch’s June 2025 report describes the order as restricting federal funding for institutions that provide or research gender-affirming care and cutting off access through federal programs. These provisions support an account of the administration’s federal restrictions and policy direction. They do not establish that every form of care was eliminated nationwide, that providers were criminally prohibited from offering care, or that a complete federal ban had taken effect. The narrower title and description therefore identify the signed order and its stated directives without claiming universal implementation or consequences beyond the cited sources.

account1_proposal.proposed_title: Pompeo Invoked an Emergency for $8.1 Billion in Arms Transfers to Three Countries
account1_proposal.proposed_description_short: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo invoked an emergency to expedite 22 arms transfers worth about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Jordan.
account1_proposal.proposed_description_medium: Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced on May 24, 2019, that he had made an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers totaling about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. He cited deterring Iran and building partner self-defense capacity. The action bypassed the ordinary congressional review period.
account1_proposal.proposed_description_long: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed the State Department to complete immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. Pompeo put their combined value at approximately $8.1 billion and said the transfers were intended to deter Iranian aggression and strengthen partner self-defense. A contemporaneous CNN report explained that invoking the emergency allowed the administration to expedite the sales without the ordinary congressional review period. The event was broader than the original title’s two named recipients: Jordan was also included. These sources establish the procedural action, approximate total and stated rationale. They do not provide in the cited press statement a full transfer-by-transfer list of weapons and services, or document the outcome of every congressional response. The revised text states the three recipients and attributes the rationale to the administration without treating it as independently proven or implying every transfer was delivered.

preserved_fields.title: Protest Masking Criminalization - Facial Recognition Enforcement and Identity Exposure
preserved_fields.description_short: Protest Masking Criminalization - Facial Recognition Enforcement and Identity Exposure
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump's administration implemented systematic criminalization of face coverings at protests by expanding police powers to ban masks and require identity exposure, using facial recognition technology to identify and prosecute demonstrators while creating 'chilling effects' that deterred disabled activists, religious minorities, and political dissidents from exercising constitutional assembly rights. The masking ban represented weaponization of identification technology against vulnerable protest participants, including disabled activists who relied on face coverings to avoid infection, Muslim women wearing niqabs, and dissidents protesting outside foreign embassies who faced retaliation from authoritarian regimes if identified by surveillance systems. The systematic exposure requirements violated privacy rights and religious freedom by forcing removal of face coverings during protests, with police empowered to arrest anyone refusing to comply while legal exemptions for religious or health reasons were only available after arrest, ensuring widespread detention of innocent individuals. The protest masking criminalization aligned with global authoritarian tactics, with countries like Hungary using facial recognition to enforce bans on LGBTQ+ Pride events by identifying participants for fines and imprisonment, demonstrating how identification requirements served to restrict civic freedoms and intensify exclusion of marginalized communities. Trump's masking ban represented what civil liberties organizations called continuation of 'wave of anti-protest laws that are shutting down ways we can speak up,' following previous restrictions on 'noisy' protests and vague locking-on laws that gave police 'almost-unlimited powers to crack down on protests and arrest demonstrators.' The facial recognition enforcement violated Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable surveillance while creating systematic intimidation designed to prevent political participation by vulnerable communities who required anonymity protection to safely exercise constitutional rights without facing retaliation, persecution, or violence.

proposed_fields.title: DOJ Intervened in Manafort’s Detention Placement After His Lawyer Raised Rikers Concerns
proposed_fields.description_short: Jeffrey Rosen contacted Manhattan prosecutors after Manafort’s lawyer objected to possible Rikers detention; Manafort stayed in federal custody.
proposed_fields.description_medium: NBC News reported in June 2019 that Paul Manafort’s lawyer asked federal officials to keep him in federal custody, citing health and safety concerns about Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen contacted Manhattan prosecutors and attached the lawyer’s letter. Manafort was held in federal custody in Manhattan rather than transferred to Rikers; the reporting does not establish that DOJ issued a formal order barring the transfer.
proposed_fields.description_long: In June 2019, Manhattan prosecutors were preparing to prosecute Paul Manafort on New York state charges while he was serving a federal sentence. NBC News, citing contemporaneous reporting and officials, said Manafort’s lawyer asked the Bureau of Prisons to keep him in federal custody because of concerns about his health and safety at Rikers Island. Deputy Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen then contacted Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance’s office, attached the lawyer’s letter, and asked for its response. Vance’s office said it had not proposed housing Manafort at Rikers and took no position on whether he should remain in federal custody. Federal officials ultimately kept Manafort in federal custody at the Metropolitan Correctional Center while making him available to state prosecutors. The available accounts support DOJ involvement in the placement decision after a defense request, but not the original claim that DOJ independently ordered Manafort kept out of Rikers. The record also does not establish political direction from Trump.

proposed_fields.title: ICE Official Testified Tiger Team Reviewed Student Protester Leads from Canary Mission
proposed_fields.description_short: Peter Hatch testified that an ICE team reviewed thousands of protester names and sent roughly 100–200 reports to the State Department.
proposed_fields.description_medium: In July 2025 trial testimony, ICE official Peter Hatch described a “Tiger Team” formed to research student-protester leads. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s daily report says the team reviewed a Canary Mission list of about 5,000 names and compiled more than 100 reports. Hatch said the team also used other sources, including Betar, and sent reports to the State Department for possible action. The testimony does not show that every listed person was targeted or deported.
proposed_fields.description_long: During the July 2025 trial in American Association of University Professors v. Rubio, Peter Hatch, an ICE Homeland Security Investigations intelligence official, testified about a specialized “Tiger Team” formed in March to investigate student protesters. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s contemporaneous trial update says Hatch described a list of roughly 5,000 people identified on Canary Mission and more than 100 resulting reports. Other reporting on the testimony says Hatch described using leads from multiple sources, including Betar, and that reports were submitted to the State Department, which would decide whether to take action. This supports a narrower account of an investigative process described in court testimony. It does not establish that the online list was an official government blacklist, that all 5,000 people were investigated in the same way, or that every subject faced removal or another enforcement action. The prior title’s use of “anti-war” and its unqualified statement that ICE used a blacklist overstate the evidence; the replacement attributes the process to Hatch’s testimony and identifies the documented scale.

uncertainty: The testimony does not establish an official government blacklist or that all named people were investigated, targeted for removal or deported.

staged_description.description_long: In late February 2026, Kari Lake reinstated a deferred-resignation program for employees of the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM), the federal agency that oversees Voice of America and other international broadcasters. A court filing states that employees could resign immediately while continuing to receive pay through September 5, 2026, and had until March 9 to accept. The filing also quotes an agency message saying that an August 2025 reduction-in-force was suspended by court order, while USAGM still intended to carry out a significant reduction when it could. A federal judge later ruled that Lake had unlawfully served as acting head during much of 2025 and voided actions taken during that period, including mass-layoff measures. That ruling concerns Lake’s appointment and prior actions; the cited reports do not say how many employees accepted this deferred-resignation offer or measure any loss of broadcasting or national-security capability attributable to it. The evidence supports the offer, its terms and its staffing context, but not the original title’s claim that the program itself hurt national security.

preserved_fields.description_short: Agricultural Sector Devastated: China Soybean Exports Collapse 72%, $14.9B Loss
preserved_fields.description_long: China's retaliatory tariffs in 2025 reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China from $24.5 billion in 2024 to just $8.4 billion in 2025, a two-thirds decline and the lowest annual figure in over two decades, per NDSU Agricultural Trade Monitor analysis. NDSU estimated the annualized China-specific agricultural export shortfall at $14.9 billion — 41% larger than the $10.6 billion shortfall during the 2018–2019 trade war. Soybeans accounted for $6.8 billion of the loss; beef and cotton each contributed $1.3 billion; corn $333 million; and tree nuts $964 million. For the first time in more than 20 years, Chinese importers purchased no soybeans from the U.S. autumn 2025 harvest, forcing American farmers to store their crops as prices fell to a five-year low. Brazil's soybean exports to China hit record levels in 2025, topping 85 million metric tons — an 18% increase — as U.S. market share evaporated.

account1_proposal.proposed_medium: At a September 22, 2017, rally in Huntsville, Alabama, Trump urged NFL owners to remove players who knelt during the national anthem, using the phrase “Get that son of a bitch off the field” and saying “He’s fired.” The transcript supports the insult and call for dismissal; it does not describe physical violence.
account1_proposal.proposed_long: The official transcript of Donald Trump’s September 22, 2017, campaign rally for Senator Luther Strange in Huntsville, Alabama, records remarks about NFL players who knelt during the national anthem. Trump asked whether owners should say, “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now,” and added, “He’s fired. He’s fired!” He also urged offended fans to leave stadiums. The transcript directly supports reporting the insult and his call for owners to dismiss protesting players. The event should be described as a political rally statement, not as physical violence or a specific threat of bodily harm. The quoted remarks do not substantiate claims about what teams subsequently did or how every player protest was treated. The record identifies this as a campaign rally for Senator Luther J. Strange III. It is not a report of NFL discipline or league action; it records Trump’s proposed response and his suggested fan response that night.

staged_description.description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14251, titled “Exclusions From Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs,” on March 27, 2025. The executive order also includes mechanisms for agency heads to identify further qualifying subdivisions under its terms. The supplied Project 2025 and labor-group sources provide policy context, but the official order and OPM memo establish what was enacted. source_proposal.corrected_long: After the White House revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass in November 2018, CNN and Acosta filed suit. On November 16, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted temporary relief requiring the pass to be restored. CNN’s contemporaneous report and the hearing transcript describe the basis as a likely Fifth Amendment due-process violation: the government had not provided adequate notice and an opportunity to respond before revoking the credential. The judge did not decide the First Amendment claim, and the temporary order was not a final ruling on the merits. The White House later restored Acosta’s pass, but that later action does not convert the temporary order into a final constitutional judgment. The evidence reviewed here also does not establish that a disputed video was the sole cause of the revocation or that media experts had definitively debunked it. The corrected account is limited to the revocation, temporary judicial restoration, and the legal ground the judge addressed. Claims about motive, video provenance, or a final finding that both amendments were violated require separate evidence.

staged_description.title: DOJ Lists Trump’s 2021 Commutation of Matthew Antione Canady
staged_description.description_short: DOJ Lists Trump’s 2021 Commutation of Matthew Antione Canady
staged_description.description_medium: The Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney lists Matthew Antione Canady under commutations granted on January 19, 2021. The official table identifies his Southern District of Iowa case, an original 262-month prison term as amended in 2014, five years of supervised release, and a cocaine-base conspiracy conviction. It does not state the replacement sentence or release conditions, so the amount of relief remains unknown.
staged_description.description_long: The Department of Justice Office of the Pardon Attorney’s official table of commutations granted by Donald Trump places Matthew Antione Canady under January 19, 2021. It identifies the Southern District of Iowa case and records a 262-month term of imprisonment, as amended by a December 22, 2014 order, followed by five years of supervised release. The listed offense is conspiracy to distribute at least 50 grams of cocaine base. This verifies that Canady appears on the administration’s commutations list and identifies the underlying sentence; it does not give the replacement prison term, whether the commutation was to time served, a release date, or the remaining supervision terms. The linked clemency-record PDF should be inspected for those details before describing the practical effect. A commutation changes punishment but is distinct from a pardon of the conviction. The corrected account can state the grant and original case facts while clearly noting that the public summary alone does not quantify the relief. It should not imply that Canady’s conviction was erased or that the commutation resulted in immediate release.

reviewed_account1_fields.proposed_title: Steven Levitsky Described U.S. Democracy Under Trump as Competitive Authoritarianism
reviewed_account1_fields.proposed_claim: In an April 22, 2025 NPR interview, Steven Levitsky said the United States had crossed into “competitive authoritarianism”; this is his assessment, not a verified finding that constitutional government ended.
reviewed_account1_fields.proposed_short: In an April 2025 NPR interview, Steven Levitsky said the U.S. had crossed into “competitive authoritarianism.”
reviewed_account1_fields.proposed_medium: In an April 22, 2025, NPR Fresh Air interview, Harvard political scientist Steven Levitsky said the United States was “no longer living in a democratic regime” and had crossed into “competitive authoritarianism.” He cited government retaliation risks and attacks or threats involving critics and institutions. These statements report Levitsky’s assessment; they do not establish a formal end to constitutional government.
reviewed_account1_fields.proposed_long: NPR’s Fresh Air interviewed Harvard political scientist Steven Levitsky on April 22, 2025, about American democracy under President Donald Trump. Levitsky said that, in his view, the country was “no longer living in a democratic regime” and had crossed into “competitive authoritarianism.” He pointed to what he described as a cost to publicly opposing the government, including attacks or threats involving law firms, company leaders, media, universities, nongovernmental organizations and individual critics. This account attributes those conclusions and examples to Levitsky. The interview supports reporting his assessment of democratic backsliding; it does not establish that all constitutional checks were eliminated, that the republic formally ended, or that permanent autocracy was achieved. The interview does not establish a completed 248-year constitutional collapse. Levitsky also called the situation mild compared with other cases, reversible, and said he was pessimistic in the short term.

proposed_fields.description_short: AP reported that at least 16 Epstein-related files disappeared from DOJ’s public webpage less than a day after posting.
proposed_fields.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that at least 16 files disappeared from the Justice Department’s public webpage for Jeffrey Epstein records less than a day after they were posted in December 2025. The missing set included a photograph showing Donald Trump with Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell. DOJ said materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted, but did not explain the removal. proposed_fields.description_long: On December 20, 2025, the Associated Press reported that at least 16 files were no longer accessible on the Justice Department’s public webpage for records related to Jeffrey Epstein, less than a day after they had been posted. The files included images of paintings and a photograph showing Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell among other photographs in a drawer. AP also reported gaps in the release, including FBI interviews with survivors and internal Justice Department memoranda about charging decisions. DOJ did not explain why the files disappeared. The department said that photos and other materials would continue to be reviewed and redacted as it received additional information. This establishes a reported change in what the public could access online and an unresolved explanation from the department. It does not establish that the files were destroyed, that the removal was permanent, or that it was intended to protect Trump or shape a political narrative. The available report supplies no evidence for the former title’s claim that the episode rewarded narrative control or caused a lasting institutional crisis. A later record of restoration, a DOJ explanation or evidence of decision-making would be needed to assess motive and consequences.

preserved_fields.title: SEC Drops 60%+ of Crypto Enforcement Cases in Mass Regulatory Capitulation
preserved_fields.description_short: SEC Drops 60%+ of Crypto Enforcement Cases in Mass Regulatory Capitulation
preserved_fields.description_long: Within weeks of Trump's inauguration, the Securities and Exchange Commission under acting chair Mark Uyeda began systematically dropping enforcement actions against the crypto industry, which had spent more than $100 million supporting Trump's election. By February 21, 2025, the SEC dismissed its nearly two-year case against Coinbase, the largest U.S. crypto exchange, which had been charged with operating as an unregistered securities exchange. On March 20, 2025, the SEC dropped its four-year case against Ripple Labs and its XRP token. The agency also dropped or froze cases against Kraken, Gemini, Binance, and Robinhood. A December 2025 New York Times investigation found that the SEC had eased up on more than 60% of the crypto cases that were in progress at the start of Trump's second term — a retreat from a single industry with no legal precedent. The investigation into Justin Sun, who had invested $45 million in Trump's World Liberty Financial, was settled in March 2025 for $10 million with no admission of wrongdoing, after being paused following his WLF investment. Senator Elizabeth Warren demanded explanations for the apparent connection between Sun's investment in the Trump family business and the SEC's decision to drop its case against him. The mass regulatory pullback directly enriched the crypto industry that had funded Trump's election while benefiting the Trump family, which held billions in crypto assets subject to SEC oversight.

This is an attributed investigative account, not a reproduced federal case file or court finding. Later articles cite Barrett’s original reporting; they do not independently corroborate every allegation.

proposed_fields.description_short: Trump said Arizona officials were trying to steal the election after Maricopa County reported ballot-machine problems.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On November 8, 2022, Donald Trump posted that Maricopa County voting machines were not counting ballots and said, “They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported printer and tabulator problems at some vote centers. A judge rejected a request to extend voting hours, finding no evidence that voters had been prevented from casting ballots. The equipment failures do not establish fraud or a stolen result.
proposed_fields.description_long: During Election Day on November 8, 2022, Maricopa County reported problems with ballot-on-demand printers and tabulators at some vote centers. Donald Trump used the reports to make a specific public accusation. In a post that afternoon he said some machines were not counting votes, then wrote: “People of Arizona: Don’t get out of line until you cast your vote. They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported the machine problems and the fraud claims made by Trump and other election deniers. In a related court proceeding, a judge rejected a Republican request to extend polling hours because the party had not shown that voters were prevented from casting ballots. Maricopa County’s post-election report documents equipment problems and how ballots were handled; those problems are not evidence that votes were changed or that the election was stolen. The original title’s reference to midterm losses is misleading because Trump’s cited post was made before the results were known. This draft records the statement and the verified dispute without endorsing its allegation.

proposed_fields.description_long: On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States,” revising the January order. Iraq was no longer among the six countries covered by the entry suspension. The order specified an effective time of March 16, 2017. These details are supported by the official Federal Register publication of the order. This correction describes the executive action itself and does not fold later district-court injunctions and appellate proceedings into one event. The supplied Associated Press URL concerns an unrelated fact-check and is not evidence for the order. Any account of the separate litigation would need citations to each order and opinion and should distinguish the Hawaii and Maryland cases from their appellate proceedings.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017
proposed_fields.description_short: The 2017 law lowered the corporate tax rate to 21% and included a temporary deduction for qualified business income.
proposed_fields.description_medium: Donald Trump signed Public Law 115-97, commonly called the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, on December 22, 2017. The statute changed individual and business tax rules; the Joint Committee on Taxation says it lowered the corporate rate from a graduated 15–35% structure to 21% and temporarily allowed a deduction for qualified business income. The entry avoids an unqualified claim about who benefited most.
proposed_fields.description_long: Donald Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017; the enacted measure is Public Law 115-97. The law changed both individual and business tax rules. In its 2019 distributional analysis, the Joint Committee on Taxation describes the reduction of the corporate income-tax rate from a graduated structure ranging from 15 percent to 35 percent to a flat 21 percent. It also describes a temporary deduction for qualified business income. The JCT report compares the act’s distributional effects with the law in effect before enactment and provides separate analysis of business-tax provisions. These are concrete provisions that can be described from the statute and JCT analysis. The sources do not justify the prior short description’s broad characterization that benefits were “skewed” toward corporations and high-income earners without identifying a particular year, measure, and distributional table. This entry therefore states the signing date and selected statutory changes, while leaving broader distributional conclusions to a clearly specified analysis rather than treating them as self-evident.

uncertainty: The broad “skewed toward corporations and high-income earners” characterization lacks a specified year, metric or cited distributional result.

proposed_fields.description_short: Trump said the United States would not become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty; the country had signed but not ratified it.
proposed_fields.description_medium: In an April 29, 2019 message to the Senate, President Donald Trump said the United States would not become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty and described withdrawing the U.S. signature. The United States had signed the treaty in 2013 but had not ratified it. In July 2019, the government told the UN depositary it did not intend to become a party and had no legal obligations arising from the signature. This was not withdrawal from a treaty the United States had joined.
proposed_fields.description_long: President Donald Trump’s April 29, 2019 message to the Senate said the United States would not become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty and addressed withdrawing the U.S. signature. The United States signed the treaty in 2013 but did not ratify it, so it was not a party withdrawing from a binding treaty. The UN Treaty Collection records a U.S. communication received on July 18, 2019, stating that the country did not intend to become a party and had no legal obligations arising from its signature. The official records support the decision and later depositary notice. They do not support describing the action as withdrawal from treaty-party status. The supplied White House archive URL is retained for the presidential message; the UN depositary notice directly confirms the legal status and communication. This account omits the unsupported April 26 convention venue/date because the mapped sources establish the April 29 message and July notice, not that earlier speaking event.

uncertainty: The U.S. was not a treaty party and did not withdraw from a binding treaty. The supplied archive source does not substantiate the April 26 venue/date used in prior prose.

proposal.proposed_title: Trump Pardons Faustino Bernadett
proposal.proposed_description_short: Trump pardoned Faustino Bernadett on January 19, 2021; DOJ lists his federal conviction, sentence, fine, and surrender date.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: The Justice Department records President Donald Trump’s January 19, 2021 pardon of Faustino Bernadett. Its clemency table lists a Central District of California conviction for misprision of a felony, a 15-month prison sentence, one year of supervised release, a $60,000 fine, and a February 26, 2021 surrender date. The record does not explain the pardon decision.
proposal.proposed_description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency record states that President Donald Trump pardoned Faustino Bernadett on January 19, 2021. DOJ identifies a Central District of California case and a conviction for misprision of a felony. The clemency table lists a 15-month prison sentence, one year of supervised release, a $60,000 fine, and a surrender date of February 26, 2021. The separate grant document confirms the pardon date and summarizes the case and sentence. These records support a factual account of the pardon and the listed court disposition. They do not describe the conduct behind the conviction, explain why Trump selected Bernadett, or document an exchange, favoritism, or corruption. The prior “Corrupt Pardons” classification therefore is not supported by the supplied evidence and is removed from this proposed draft. The neutral title describes the established event without implying a motive. A case narrative or contemporaneous clemency rationale would be needed to make claims about the underlying conduct or reason for clemency.
